title: The second Trump presidency is a world-historic failure
gist: Noah Smith argues Trump's second term has already failed in the court of public opinion: WSJ approval of 37% is the lowest of any president heading into midterms since 1990, Republicans now net-disapprove of his handling of the cost of living, and Kalshi markets favor Democrats to take the House and give them better-than-even odds in the Senate. (The available text is the free preview; the paywalled section on why Trump failed is not included.)

insights.claim: A WSJ poll (Sept 16-21, 2026) puts Trump's approval at 37% with 61% disapproval, the lowest of any president heading into midterms in WSJ polling dating to 1990; 60% say the economy is worse under Trump versus 25% better.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Below G.W. Bush's 39% in 2006, a midterm where his party lost both chambers, pointing to a large anti-incumbent swing in November 2026.
insights.quote: The lowest approval any president heading into midterms in WSJ polling dating to 1990.
insights.locator: Trump is a failure in the eyes of the nation

insights.claim: Reuters/Ipsos (Sept 17-20, 2026) shows Trump at 32% approve / 66% disapprove, his lowest Ipsos reading in either term, with only 17% approving on cost of living.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Cost of living is the administration's weakest flank, raising pressure for populist affordability measures before the vote.

insights.claim: For the first time, Trump's net approval on cost of living is negative among Republicans: 44% approve, 51% disapprove.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Base erosion on the economy suggests weaker GOP turnout and further downside for Republican midterm prospects.
insights.quote: First time his net approval on the issue has been negative among Republicans.
insights.locator: Trump’s approval among Republicans on handling

insights.claim: Smith notes a modest but growing number of 2024 Trump voters now say they never voted for him, and Republicans increasingly say they support the party rather than Trump himself, per Echelon Insights.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Signals weakening of Trump's personal grip on the GOP, which could shape post-midterm party positioning.
insights.locator: Hilariously, a modest but growing number

insights.claim: Kalshi prediction markets are increasingly sure Democrats will take the House and give them a better-than-even chance of winning the Senate despite a very difficult map.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Markets are pricing a meaningful chance of unified Democratic control of Congress, which would sharply limit the administration's legislative agenda from 2027.
insights.quote: Prediction markets are increasingly sure that Dems will take the House
insights.locator: But nevertheless, the GOP is going to suffer

insights.claim: Smith cautions that Senate polls may overstate Democratic gains, but notes polls have understated Democratic support in special elections since Trump returned to power.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Polling error has historically skewed against Democrats this cycle, so the risk to Democratic odds may be smaller than feared.
insights.quote: polls have ended up understating Democratic support in special elections since Trump returned to power

insights.claim: Trump has promised $5,000 checks to every US citizen if Republicans win the midterms, but Smith says the offer is falling flat and actively driving voters away.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A pledged large-scale fiscal transfer is a potential deficit and inflation wildcard if Republicans hold Congress, though voters are not rewarding it.
insights.quote: these wild bribe attempts are falling decidedly flat — in fact, they’re actively driving voters away
insights.locator: Trump has resorted to desperately promising

insights.claim: Despite Democrats being in disarray over Israel/Palestine and public skepticism of 'woke' ideology, voters who trusted Republicans more on many issues in 2025 now tend to trust Democrats on the economy and immigration, per Lakshya Jain.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A reversal of issue ownership on the economy and immigration within a year is an unusually large shift in the political landscape.
insights.quote: The GOP was more popular than the Dems as of one year ago; now that has reversed.
insights.locator: All this is all the more remarkable

insights.claim: Peter Thiel, a Tech Right godfather, has distanced himself from Trump, saying the administration was crazier and more dangerous than he thought and is staffed by not very smart but very loyal people.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Defections by tech-industry backers could weaken the Tech Right's alignment with the administration and its policy influence.
insights.quote: administration is… staffed by not very smart but very loyal people
insights.locator: Even some of Trump’s most prominent allies

insights.claim: Smith allows that Trump's term could someday look like a success if winning the AI race proves paramount and his decision to stall AI regulation outweighs everything else, but rejects 'too early to tell' reasoning.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Light-touch AI regulation is the one policy Smith flags as potentially historically consequential in Trump's favor.
insights.quote: Perhaps winning the AI race will prove to be so much more important than everything else
insights.locator: I can’t rule out the possibility

insights.claim: Smith calls Trump's second term an already-realized world-historic failure in public opinion, driven by avoidable errors made for ideological and personal reasons.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frames the political environment as structurally adverse for the incumbent party heading into 2027-28.
insights.quote: Trump simply made a bunch of avoidable errors, for a mix of ideological and personal reasons
insights.locator: But I don’t find it very useful
